_metadata.name: 24 Solar Terms (二十四节气)
_metadata.convention: Each term marks the Sun's tropical ecliptic longitude at a multiple of 15°
_metadata.grouping: 12 'sectional' (节) terms and 12 'mid' (气 / zhōngqì) terms, alternating
source_notes: The 24 Solar Terms are the canonical seasonal markers of the Chinese calendar.
Each term begins when the Sun's tropical ecliptic longitude reaches an exact multiple of 15°.
Unlike the lunar-mansion system, solar terms are TROPICAL — anchored to the equinoxes and solstices, not to stars.
Modern China still publishes these on every calendar; UNESCO inscribed them on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2016.
_metadata.epistemic_tag: [SOURCE: Chinese classical astronomy — Han dynasty canon]

terms.notes: First of the 24 terms. The day the Sun reaches 315° tropical longitude. Marks the astronomical start of spring; agricultural year begins. Damanhurian counterpart: roughly midway between Winter Solstice and Spring Equinox.
Snow gives way to rain. Soil begins to thaw in temperate latitudes.
Hibernating insects emerge. Thunder begins. The first stirrings — connects thematically to the 'dragon root awakening' of Saga Dawa one month later.
Equal day and night. The Sun crosses the celestial equator going north. Damanhurian Great Rite: Spring Equinox (Month 7, OSIRIS — The Resurrected).
Tomb-Sweeping Day (清明节) — major Chinese ancestral festival. The air is clear, sky bright, vegetation greens. Tea harvest begins (清明茶 Qingming tea).
Rains nourish the grain. Sowing season for many crops in temperate China.
Astronomical start of summer. Falls just before Saga Dawa typically begins. Yang energy ascendant.
Grains begin to fill out but are not yet full. Falls during Saga Dawa in most years.
Wheat ripens; rice transplanting. The bearded grain — wheat awns visible.
Longest day, shortest night. The Sun reaches its highest declination. Damanhurian Great Rite: Summer Solstice (Month 10, SET — The Destroyer / the peak that initiates decline).
Heat begins to build. The 'three fú' (三伏) period of greatest heat begins around this time.
Peak heat. The dog days of summer. Monsoon at its strongest in subtropical China.
Astronomical start of autumn. Heat persists but yin begins to grow. Traditional 'autumn-jin' (秋筋) marker.
Heat retreats; cooler mornings. 'Chǔ' means to dwell or pause — heat pauses its dominance.
Morning dew becomes visibly white. First clear sign of approaching cold.

Equal day and night. Sun crosses celestial equator going south. Damanhurian Great Rite: Autumn Equinox (Month 1, ISIS — The Gatherer). The Damanhurian Divine Year begins at the New Moon nearest this term.
Dew turns cold. Migratory birds head south.
First frost in northern China. Close to the Damanhurian Day of the Dead (Month 2, SADAM).
Astronomical start of winter. Field work ends; storage begins.
First snow possible in northern China.
Heavy snow common. Deep winter approaches.

Shortest day, longest night. Sun reaches lowest declination; cycle begins to ascend again. Damanhurian Great Rite: Winter Solstice (Month 4, EOROS — The Director). One of the most important festivals of the Chinese year (冬至 dumpling tradition).
Cold deepens. The 'three nines' (三九) — coldest 27 days of the year — begin around this point.
Peak cold. The final term of the year; Lìchūn (Beginning of Spring) follows.
